questions.stem: What event first creates the resistance allele in a bacterial population?

options.text: A random mutation in the genetic material
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Exposure to the antibiotic creates it
options.explanation: The drug only selects among existing variants; the allele must already exist.

options.text: The patient's immune system designs it
options.explanation: Immunity and bacterial genetics are separate systems.

options.text: Resistant bacteria invade from elsewhere
options.explanation: The taught account starts the allele with mutation inside the population.

questions.stem: What happens to bacteria lacking the resistance allele when the antibiotic is applied?

options.text: They switch to a different antibiotic
options.explanation: Individual bacteria cannot swap their own treatment.

options.text: They die, leaving the resistant carriers to thrive
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: They mutate immediately and survive
options.explanation: Mutation is random and does not answer the drug on demand.

options.text: They become dormant forever
options.explanation: The taught outcome is death of the undefended cells.

questions.stem: Why does the resistance allele become more common over generations?

options.text: Bacteria purposefully evolve to survive
options.explanation: Selection acts on existing variation without intent.

options.text: The drug breeds resistance into survivors
options.explanation: The drug filters; it does not breed anything.

options.text: Carriers reproduce more successfully and pass the allele on
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: The allele grows stronger inside each cell
options.explanation: Frequency rises through inheritance, not internal strengthening.

questions.stem: Which process does antibiotic resistance exemplify?

options.text: Genetic engineering
options.explanation: No laboratory intervenes in the taught account.

options.text: Active transport
options.explanation: That moves molecules across membranes, not populations.

options.text: Mitosis
options.explanation: Cell division alone does not explain the changing allele frequency.

options.text: Natural selection
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

questions.stem: A resistant infection fails to respond to its usual drug. What is the treatment implication?

options.text: A different antibiotic, sometimes several combined, must be used
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: The same drug at a higher dose always works
options.explanation: Resistance can defeat the usual drug outright.

options.text: No treatment is possible
options.explanation: Other antibiotics remain options.

options.text: The infection must simply run its course untreated
options.explanation: The taught account prescribes alternative drugs.

questions.stem: List the four stages that describe how antibiotic resistance spreads through a population.
questions.modelAnswer: Mutation produces the resistance allele, the antibiotic kills non-carriers, surviving carriers reproduce and pass the allele on, and the allele frequency increases each generation.

questions.stem: State why antibiotic resistance makes infections harder to control.
questions.modelAnswer: Resistant bacteria survive the usual drugs, so treatment needs a different antibiotic or several together.

questions.stem: Explain why using an antibiotic does not create resistance, even though resistance rises after treatment.
questions.modelAnswer: The resistance allele already exists through random mutation; the drug acts by natural selection, killing non-carriers, so the frequency increases rather than the drug instructing bacteria to change.

questions.stem: A patient stops a course of antibiotics early. Describe how this can raise the frequency of resistant bacteria remaining in the body.
questions.modelAnswer: Surviving bacteria include any carrying resistance alleles; with the drug gone they reproduce freely, so the resistant forms multiply and their allele frequency climbs in the population left behind.
